Dallas Statement
DAL-us STAYT-mint
noun phrase (document)
Popular name for The Statement on Social Justice and the Gospel, drafted in 2018 and associated with a meeting in Dallas, Texas. Its initial drafters included John MacArthur and a group of pastors and theologians concerned about the inroads of social-justice ideology into evangelicalism.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Dallas Statement — formally The Statement on Social Justice and the Gospel (2018) — is an evangelical confessional statement opposing the adoption of secular social-justice ideology (Critical Race Theory, intersectionality, and the broader "woke" framework) into evangelical theology and practice. Initiated by John MacArthur and a group of pastors and theologians, and signed by thousands, it consists of a preamble and fourteen articles in the "We affirm... We deny..." confessional form, addressing Scripture, the imago Dei, justice, God's law, sin, the gospel, salvation, the church, heresy, sexuality and marriage, complementarianism, race and ethnicity, and culture. Its central concern is that the categories of secular critical theory — systemic oppression, group identity, intersectional victimhood, the oppressor-oppressed binary — were being imported into evangelical churches and seminaries in ways that distort the biblical doctrines of sin (individual guilt before God, not collective racial guilt), salvation (deliverance from sin and wrath, not from social structures), the church (one new humanity in Christ, not a coalition of identity groups), and justice (rendering to each his due under God's law, not the redistribution of power along identity lines). The statement affirms the biblical anthropology of one-in-Adam (Rom 5:12) and one-in-Christ (Gal 3:28) against the race-as-master-category framework of Critical Race Theory (the dictionary's critical-race-theory entry). From the Reformed standpoint the dictionary holds, the Dallas Statement is a faithful confessional response to the specific error of woke ideology's entry into the church, anchored in the biblical categories of sin, grace, and the heart. It was attacked as dismissive of real injustice and divisive within evangelicalism; the dictionary commends its substance while affirming that genuine injustice must be opposed on biblical, not critical-theory, grounds.

DALLAS STATEMENT, noun phrase. Popular name for The Statement on Social Justice and the Gospel (2018).

Initiated by John MacArthur and a group of pastors and theologians; signed by thousands.

Preamble plus fourteen articles in "We affirm... We deny..." confessional form.

Opposes the import of secular social-justice ideology (CRT, intersectionality, the woke framework) into evangelical theology.

Affirms biblical anthropology — one-in-Adam (Rom 5:12), one-in-Christ (Gal 3:28) — against race-as-master-category.

📖 Key Scripture

Romans 5:12 — "Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned."

Galatians 3:28 — "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus."

Micah 6:8 — "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?"

Ezekiel 18:20 — "The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Dallas Statement is corrupted when caricatured as indifference to real injustice, when treated as a complete social ethic rather than a boundary against a specific error, or when used as a tribal-loyalty test rather than received as a confession of biblical anthropology and justice.

expand to see more

Indifference-to-injustice caricature. The statement was widely attacked as dismissive of genuine racial injustice and as a refuge for those who wished to ignore real wrongs. The document itself affirms that God's law requires justice, that partiality is sin, and that genuine injustice must be opposed (Micah 6:8). Its concern is not to deny injustice but to insist that injustice be defined and opposed on biblical grounds — individual guilt and individual righteousness before God's law (Ezek 18:20) — rather than on the Critical Race Theory grounds of collective racial guilt and group-identity victimhood. The statement opposes a particular framework for understanding injustice, not the opposition to injustice itself.

Loyalty-test misreading. Like the Nashville Statement, the Dallas Statement became, in some quarters, a tribal-loyalty marker — a line that sorted evangelicals into camps. Adam Johns's own blog work tracking signers' later trajectories makes the wiser point: the statement is a faithful confession of biblical anthropology against woke ideology, and subscribing it is good, but the test of a man's fidelity is the settled trajectory of his teaching and life, not his name on the document. The dictionary commends the statement's substance — the biblical categories of sin, the heart, and justice under God's law — while refusing to make a signature the measure of a man.
